title: Why exact search stops scaling

kcs.statement: Exact search costs N·d per query; ANN indexes trade a little recall for large speedups, measured against an exact baseline.

visual_fit.why: Exact search cost grows in a straight line with the number of vectors; a chart makes the scale visible.

misconceptions.statement: A vector database returns the exact nearest neighbours.

md: The search from the Basics layer compares the query with **every** vector. That's called *flat* or *exact* search. For $N$ vectors of $d$ dimensions it costs about $N \times d$ multiply-adds per query.

- 10,000 chunks × 384 dims ≈ 3.8 million operations: **instant**.
- 10,000,000 chunks × 768 dims ≈ **7.7 billion** operations, and $10^7 \times 768 \times 4$ bytes ≈ **30.7 GB** of float32 read from memory **per query**. At typical server memory bandwidth of tens of GB/s, that's on the order of a second per query, before you serve 1,000 users at once.

[[ANN]] (approximate nearest neighbour) indexes avoid looking at most vectors. They return the **probably** nearest neighbours in milliseconds. You pay with **recall**, measured against exact search: an ANN index at 0.95 recall@10 returns 9.5 of the true top-10 on average.

block.md: Almost every production vector database runs ANN, so results are **approximate by design**, and the index has knobs that trade speed for recall. Measure recall against an exact baseline on a sample of queries.
block.title: “The vector DB returns the true nearest neighbours”

block.md: Up to tens or hundreds of thousands of vectors, exact search with a good matrix library (or a GPU) is often fast enough. It is exact, simple, and needs no tuning. Reach for ANN when latency or cost forces you to.
block.title: Don't reach for ANN too early

question.prompt_md: How much memory do **1,000,000** vectors of **1,536** float32 dimensions take? Answer in GB (1 GB = 10⁹ bytes), 1 decimal.

common_wrong.why_md: That counts 1 byte per dimension. float32 is 4 bytes.

question.solution_md: $10^6 \times 1536 \times 4 = 6.144 \times 10^9$ bytes ≈ **6.1 GB**, before any index overhead.

block.title: Exact search reads every vector, every query
block.alt: A line chart of memory read per query against vectors stored, from 0 to 10 million, for float32 vectors. At 768 dimensions it grows to 30.7 GB per query at 10 million vectors; at 384 dimensions it reaches 15.4 GB.
block.caption_md: Memory read per query = $N \times d \times 4$ bytes for float32 vectors. At tens of GB/s of memory bandwidth, the top of this chart is about a second per query.

recap.formula: exact cost per query = N · d multiply-adds
recap.pitfall: Measure ANN recall against an exact baseline, or you cannot tell what you gave up.
